<section id="overview" class="content-section">

## What is Danaher Triangle System?

**The Danaher Triangle System is a BJJGraph study framework connecting triangle entry and control with the different orientations an opponent's movement can create.**

Triangles Enter The System is a direct companion for comparing front, opposite, rear, side and reverse triangle situations. The vendor syllabus includes setup work, transitions from preliminary control to a completed configuration, and connections to arm attacks. This makes it useful when a familiar front-triangle attempt changes shape during a defensive turn.

The following plan is BJJGraph's own way to organise practice. Start with one configuration and learn to recognise what is enclosed and what remains free. Then compare a neighbouring orientation without assuming that every change preserves a viable choke. The linked submission pages support further reading, while a coach or the course demonstrations supplies the actual movement details.

</section>

<section id="key-principles" class="content-section">

## Core Principles
- Recognise the controlled head-and-arm relationship before naming the triangle variation.
- Separate initial trapping from securing the intended configuration.
- Use orientation changes as information about control, not as automatic finishing opportunities.
- Keep arm attacks available only when their own control requirements are present.
- Choose entries that fit your current guard or top game.
- Do not force the neck or rush a transition to make a loose triangle work.


</section>

<section id="key-components" class="content-section">

## Key Components
**Initial head-and-arm capture** (Distinguish an entry opportunity from a secured position.)
Study the moment one arm is enclosed and compare that initial capture with the control required for the chosen triangle configuration.

**Configuration completion** (Locate the most fragile part of the transition.)
Observe whether changing leg position preserves the original capture or lets the defender recover their arm.

**Orientation recognition** (Make variation selection a response to the actual position.)
Name the attacker's relationship to the defender in the front, rear or side situation being studied.

**Arm-attack branches** (Evaluate an alternative without treating it as guaranteed.)
Identify when a controlled arm offers a separate attack and when changing objectives would release the entire triangle position.



</section>

<section id="implementation-sequence" class="content-section">

## Implementation Sequence
1. **Choose a front-triangle starting point**: Use a familiar guard entry and stop once the head-and-arm capture is recognisable.


2. **Compare capture and configuration**: Rehearse the move from preliminary capture to the intended leg configuration. Let the defender show where their arm could become free.


3. **Introduce a slow turn**: Allow one coached change of orientation and name the triangle situation that remains, if any.


4. **Check the alternative arm attack**: Pause when an arm becomes available. Decide whether its control supports a separate attack or whether retaining the triangle is preferable.


5. **Return to the entry**: Repeat from the same guard context with either of the agreed reactions. Stop when control disappears and record which transition needs review.




</section>

<section id="common-obstacles" class="content-section hide-minimal">

## What Challenges Will You Face?
- **The attacker names a variation but cannot explain the control.**: Describe where the head and enclosed arm sit before rehearsing its finish.
- **The arm escapes while the legs are reconfigured.**: Shorten the transition and check the initial capture with a coach.
- **Every defensive turn triggers a new submission attempt.**: Add a deliberate pause to assess whether either control remains usable.
- **Too many triangle variations are studied simultaneously.**: Compare one starting configuration with one neighbouring orientation until their differences are clear.


</section>

<section id="assessment-metrics" class="content-section">

## How to Measure Your Progress
**Capture recognition**: Assess whether the initial head-and-arm relationship is clear.
Proficiency indicators:
- Names the enclosed arm
- Recognises incomplete capture
- Can pause without squeezing


**Transition retention**: Check whether leg reconfiguration preserves the entry.
Proficiency indicators:
- Identifies arm withdrawal
- Retains a recognisable position
- Can describe the lost connection


**Orientation discrimination**: Compare two triangle situations in slow practice.
Proficiency indicators:
- Names the starting orientation
- Recognises a changed orientation
- Distinguishes a lost triangle from a variation


**Branch selection**: Observe decisions when a separate arm attack appears.
Proficiency indicators:
- Checks arm control
- Can retain the triangle instead
- Resets when neither option is secure




</section>

<section id="training-methodology" class="content-section hide-minimal">

## How to Train This System Effectively

### Drilling Approach
BJJGraph suggests comparing two snapshots: initial front-triangle capture and the intended completed configuration. Have the partner give one slow turning response and pause again. Name which control survives before considering another triangle or an arm attack. Keep the neck comfortable and use a coach to select movements suitable for both partners.

### Progression Path
**Capture** (Focus: Recognise the enclosed head-and-arm relationship.)
**Configuration** (Focus: Maintain capture while adjusting the legs.)
**Orientation** (Focus: Compare the starting triangle with one coached neighbouring form.)
**Branching** (Focus: Evaluate a retained triangle against one separate arm attack.)


### Common Mistakes
- Treating the name of a triangle as proof that it is controlled.
- Pulling on the neck to compensate for a loose configuration.
- Learning several branches before retaining the first capture.


</section>
